claims.text: Traditional fusion-welding repair is ineffective for the damaged component because of hot cracking.
A CoCrFeMnNi-based high-entropy-alloy powder is a suitable in situ filler for friction-stir repair of the unspecified parent alloy.
A friction-stir tool rotation range of 300–600 rpm is suitable for this repair.
Friction stir processing can be applied to high-entropy-alloy sheets using a non-consumable refractory-metal tool and controlled traverse parameters.
The repair process can be maintained below 0.5 times the melting temperature.
The proposed repaired material can remain stable during thermal cycling up to 900°C.
Friction stir processing induces severe plastic deformation, dynamic recrystallization, and grain refinement in the proposed repair zone.
Dynamic recrystallization during friction stir processing eliminates preexisting microcracks.
Homogeneous dispersion of the injected filler powder forms a graded transition zone between the repair overlay and parent material.
A seamless compositional gradient minimizes thermal-expansion mismatch between the repair and parent material.
Thermal-expansion mismatch can create tensile stresses that increase the susceptibility of CoCrFeMnNi welds to thermal cracking.
Solidification cracking results from the combined action of an intergranular low-melting liquid film and large tensile stress.
Traditional fusion welding generally produces hot cracking because of high-temperature gradients, compositional discontinuities, and unfavorable thermal-expansion mismatch.
The optimized repair will have a fine, homogeneous, crack-free microstructure.
The repair will provide tensile strength and ductility comparable to or better than traditional fusion-welded repairs.
The repair will provide creep resistance comparable to or better than traditional fusion-welded repairs.
Uniform filler dispersion is required for the intervention to remain effective.
Scale-up and optimization of tool design are critical to avoiding compositional inhomogeneity and obtaining reliable mechanical performance.
Cracking, significant compositional inhomogeneity, or inferior mechanical properties relative to the fusion-welded control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction allows performance significantly superior to fusion-welded repair, but the falsification rule says properties that are 'significantly different' from the fusion-welded repair falsify the hypothesis. A significantly superior result could therefore both confirm and falsify it.
